books.section: D. Debates over the Scope of Government and International Trade
Prosperity and a New World Order (1988–2000)
Reagan, H. W., Clinton, and W. (1980-2001)

stem: The debate described in the passage best illustrates which broader change in American politics?

options.text: Republicans and Democrats agreed to end all debate over trade
options.misconception: The passage shows a live argument, and trade debates ran on for decades after 1993.

options.text: The Democratic Party split between free-trade centrists and its labor base
Labor unions switched to supporting Republican candidates
options.misconception: Unions stayed in the Democratic camp even as they fought Clinton on trade.

options.text: The debate over globalization ended with the signing of NAFTA
options.misconception: Background: protesters filled Seattle in 1999 to fight the World Trade Organization, six years after NAFTA.

rationales.A: The passage is itself an argument, with critics warning factories would move. Background: the trade debate ran on for decades.
rationales.B: Background: Clinton broke with organized labor and environmental groups by embracing NAFTA, moving his party toward the center.
rationales.C: Unions fought Clinton on trade but stayed Democratic. Background: their quarrel was inside the party, not a switch of sides.
rationales.D: Background: protesters filled Seattle in 1999 to fight the World Trade Organization, six years after NAFTA was signed.
rationales.general:
1. Notice who is arguing: a Democratic president promising jobs from trade, and critics warning factories will leave.
2. Background: Clinton broke with organized labor by embracing NAFTA, moving his party toward the center.
3. That is a split inside one party, not a deal between the parties.
4. The fight did not end in 1993; it filled the streets of Seattle in 1999.
Remember: when a president fights his own base, the story is a party splitting, not two parties agreeing.

stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of President Bill Clinton's remarks on signing the North American Free Trade Agreement, December 8, 1993. Post-1929 material is paraphrased, not quoted.
stimulus.text: Paraphrase of President Bill Clinton's remarks on signing the North American Free Trade Agreement, December 8, 1993: Clinton said the agreement would tear down trade barriers among the United States, Canada, and Mexico, letting American goods, services, and investment move freely across borders. He argued that open trade would create American jobs by opening new markets, even as critics warned that factories would move to Mexico in search of cheaper labor.
